newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-AMLC Beef Weekly - Australian export prices.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-AMLC Beef Weekly - Australian export prices.

text.p: Australian Meat and Livestock Corp's (AMLC) weekly export prices are as follows:
AUSTRALIAN EXPORT PRICES TO U.S. IN U.S. CENTS/LB, CIF.
Bull (95 Chemical Lean) 99 +11 on last week
AUSTRALIAN EXPORT PRICES TO JAPAN IN U.S. CENTS/LB CIF.
Chilled grassfed fullsets 124 -7 on last week

AMLC COMMENTARY: Across inland Australia, soaring temperatures forced large numbers of stock to the saleyards. In Queensland, yardings lifted significantly causing a correction in prices, which fell between 4.0 and 8.0 cents kg liveweight.

Quality and numbers in New South Wales and Victoria were also affected by the weather and, as a result, prices were also a little weaker. By and large, export categories were the hardest hit. Generally, trade weights and feeder steer prices, although slightly down in Queensland, held firm in the other states.

In the U.S. lean manufacturing beef surged higher this week as buyers were caught short of supplies entering March, when demand improves seasonally. The effect that this buying had on prices was magnified by lower U.S. production, an easing in the U.S. domestic cow kill and tight spot market supplies of Australian and New Zealand lean beef.
Frenzied U.S. spot market activity quickly flowed to export offer prices, which finished the week 20-30 Ac/kg higher. Export prices for 90CL cow beef, at 244 Ac/kg FAX, are the highest for two years.

U.S. cow kills are likely to continue reducing, as the northern hemisphere moves out of winter into spring. Offsetting this will be larger cow meat supplies out of New Zealand as the cow run there begins in March.

Unless market conditions in Japan improve, higher U.S. prices will mean that consignments from Australia, U.S. and New Zealand to Japan are likely to contract, potentially increasing export prices in this market. While higher export prices will no doubt increase export demand for Australian supplies adding to this will be anticipated numbers out of Victoria.
Although the Japanese market remained subdued this week, there are a number of encouraging signs that this market may begin to recover soon.
Sustained improvement in Japanese consumption would raise demand for Australian cattle, hence lifting prices.
